column11:
The cleaning was described in detail, especially the difference between missing answers, "not applicable", and "pre verbal".

The cleaning mainly focuses on relabeling code though. I dont see any checks for duplicated records, agreement between GCS totals and components, or conflicting clinical responses.
column12: Yes. The figures were relevant and discussed in the report. The before and after headache plot shows the cleaning logic, the demographic plots explain which groups were explored, and the indication plots provided context for finding #2.
column13: The figures have clear captions, labeled axes, and are easy to understand. The demographic charts look good and are easy to understand. Figure 5 has very small text though. Also the model stability plots have a lot of overlapping points near zero, and are very sparse further out. The demographic plots could also be combined into one figure to save space.
column15: The finding is that there are differences in both CT scan rates and ciTBI rates across patients with different races. The two panels make the comparison easy to understand, and the sample counts are useful. Maybe some kind of uncertainty intervals could be added.
column17: The finding is that commonly cited reasons for scanning are not necessarily the ones that are associated with the highest injury rates. Evidence of skull fractures have the highest yield, while parental requests and headaches have much lower yields. The sorted bars, seperate colors for positive CT and ciTBI, and sample counts make things easy to follow. However, the patient can have more than one reason for getting a CT scan, and the figure doesn't isolate each reasons contribution.
column18:
The reality check was clear and useful. They compared their results with the original paper, and showed where the differences came from.

It is not really an independent check though, since both analyses use the same data.
column19:
The stability check was relevant to finding #1 because differences in injury severity could help explain differences between racial groups. They compared ciTBI rates within each severity group. The White-Black difference remained in the moderate and high severity groups, but slightly reversed in the low severity group.

This backs up the overall pattern, but it does not rule out other explanations or show whether or not the differences could be due to chance.
column20:
They used logistic regression and a decision tree that was limited to four levels. They used four predictors available before a CT scan, and evaluated both models on a seperate test set. Logistic regression was slightly better, and adding injury severity improved both models.

Reporting sensitivity and specificity at a chosen cutoff would have made the comparison more useful.

column13:

column15:
The charts in both panels are clean and sorted. However, I am missing the confidence intervals. Also, I don't know the meaning behind both greyed bars. 

The figure used the entire sample, so the GCS 3-13 patients as well even though the reality check says that they reproduced Kuppermann et al.'s findings when only limiting the sample to GCS 14-15. Also, "Other" is being shown in the graph but not mentioned in the text. Given that n=433 which is larger than the sample for Asian, I thought it would be worth noting what "Other" encompasses
column17: I think that the design works well as it properly shows the contrast between trauma-team requests and parent requests which is a nice insight. However, there are no confidence intervals and the dashed lines are not in the legend. Also, bars are sorted by PosCT even though ciTBI is the outcome of interest. Indications are not mutually exclusive so each bar mixes in effects of other indications
column18: Yes, the reality check was convincing and clearly described. They used Kuppermann et al. as external benchmark and diagnosed the mismatch when including GCS 3-13 patients. That they reproduce the correct sample size and the amount of ciTBI cases shows that the check was effective. However, the quantities checked only validate the cohort definition and not the gated-family cleaning that makes up most of the report's work. I don't understand why they report the caveat of using all patients but don't incorporate that finding for the findings or the models.
column19: I think that stratifying by mechanism severity is a good confounder check which also makes before and after figures easy to follow. Still, it is only a confounding check and not a perturbation of a judgment call. This is why it is less relevant to the finding. Also, it only covers finding 1 and not 2, so I don't think this is a convincing stability check.
column20: The report fits a logistic regression and a depth-4 decision tree. What I like is the restriction to information available before the CT as well as the reasoning for pairing the additive model with one that captures interactions. Issues most relate to the cohort (again, GCS 3-13 patients are included), the outcome coding (missing outcomes are treated as negatives), and the predictors leave out some strong known predictors (skull-fracture signs, GCS 14) without any justification.
